children: Kuwait’s government needs to end its monopoly of the hydrocarbon sector and allow private investment into its downstream industry, a former senior oil executive told Zawya Projects.

The move has become more imperative in the current circumstances as it will tap the sector’s surplus funds and develop the more profitable refining and petrochemical industry, said Kamil Al-Harami, former CEO of the state-owned Kuwait Petroleum International (KPI), the Gulf emirate’s downstream investment arm abroad.
Al-Harami said refined and petrochemical products are now selling at one of their highest prices, with some products exceeding the price of crude by at least $40.
He said Kuwait, a founding OPEC member, must concentrate on expansion of its downstream industry rather than increasing crude output capacity.
Although crude prices have exceeded $100, the price of some petroleum products has reached $170 a barrel, including petrol and naphtha.
“Personally, I don’t favour the idea of increasing Kuwait’s crude oil production capacity to more than three million barrels per day (bpd) in the current circumstances,” he said.

“Kuwait must focus now on the development of the downstream industry, including refining and petrochemicals as they are far more profitable…Kuwait has the chance now to do so with the help of the private sector, which has the right to participate in the development of the country’s national resources.”

Kuwait already has the second largest Arab refining capacity after Saudi Arabia, standing at around 1.45 million bpd, nearly 13 percent of the total Arab refining production of 11.5 million bpd at the end of 2025, according to the Kuwait-based Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC).
Kuwait’s refineries had a capacity of over 800,000 bpd in 2020 before the construction of the giant $16 billion Al-Zour refinery, which added around 615,000 bpd.

Kuwait has said it is planning to build a $10-billion petrochemical complex next to the southern Al-Zour refinery, with the capacity to produce nearly 2.7 million tonnes per year of aromatics and polypropylene and 1.7 million tonnes of petrol.

“Accelerating the integrated petrochemical complex project linked to the Al Zour refinery is a significant strategic step that reflects a clear path towards maximising the added value of Kuwait’s oil sector and shifting from a focus on exporting raw materials to expanding into more profitable and sustainable downstream industries,” said Ali Al-Anzi, manager of the Kuwaiti-based Al-Manakh economic centre.
He noted that the complex could be built as a joint public-private venture to ease the financial burden on the government.

“While public-private partnerships (PPP) have reached an advanced stage in various sectors, isn't it time to privatise some oil sectors to address the persistent budget deficit and leverage Kuwaiti expertise and capabilities,” Al-Harami said.

“Even if the government were to sell a portion of its shares rather than the entirety of them, what harm would there be in allowing the private sector to contribute its capital to some hydrocarbon sectors…this would allow the private sector to retain its capital and utilise it domestically, instead of investing it abroad.”
(Reporting by N Saeed; Editing by Anoop Menon)

title: Kuwait urged to let private funds into downstream sector
